subject: Jurisprudence
topic: Legal Personality: Natural vs Artificial Persons
question: What do you understand by legal personality? Distinguish between natural and artificial persons.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: In **Jurisprudence**, law regulates human conduct by conferring rights and imposing duties. However, the subject of these rights and duties is called a **person**. In ordinary language, a person means only a human being, but in law, the term has a much wider meaning. **Legal personality** is the capacity granted by law to bear rights and duties.

Therefore, law treats not only human beings as persons, but also certain **non-human entities** such as companies, corporations, idols, and universities. **Salmond** rightly observed that a person is any being whom the law regards as capable of rights and duties. Without **legal personality**, an entity cannot sue or be sued in court.

sections.heading: Meaning and Essentials of Legal Personality
paras: According to **Salmond**, a legal person is any subject-matter other than a human being to which the law attributes personality. **Austin** defines personality as the capacity to possess rights and duties. Simply put, **legal personality** is a legal fiction created by the state to recognize an entity as an independent unit in the eyes of law.

Two essential elements form a legal person: the **corpus** and the **animus**. The corpus is the body or physical structure into which the law infuses personality, such as a group of shareholders or an idol. The animus is the will or intention attributed by law, exercised through human agents like **directors** or trustees.

sections.heading: Distinction: Natural vs Artificial Persons

points.title: Creation and Origin
points.text: A **natural person** is a living human being created by nature through birth. In contrast, an **artificial person** is a creation of **law** formed through registration, statute, or legal recognition, such as a company under the Companies Act.

points.title: Physical Existence
points.text: A natural person possesses a real **physical body**, mind, and soul. An artificial person has no physical body; it is an **abstract legal fiction** that exists only in the contemplation of law and acts through **human agents**.

points.title: Lifespan and Succession
points.text: The legal personality of a natural person begins at birth and ends with **physical death**. An artificial person enjoys **perpetual succession**, meaning it continues to exist even if its members die, until dissolved by **legal process**.

points.title: Capacity and Functions
points.text: A natural person can perform all legal acts personally, including marriage and voting. An artificial person has **limited capacity** restricted by its **charter or statute**, and it cannot exercise purely personal human rights or commit **bodily crimes**.

points.title: Citizenship and Rights
points.text: A natural person can acquire **citizenship** and enjoy all constitutional fundamental rights. Under Indian law, an artificial person like a company is a **legal person**, not a citizen under **Article 19**, though it enjoys rights under Article 14.

points.title: Liability and Punishment
points.text: A natural person can be held both civilly and criminally liable, including facing **imprisonment**. An artificial person can own property, pay taxes, and face **civil damages** or criminal fines, though it cannot be physically imprisoned.

sections.tip: Draw a neat two-column comparison table in your exam after listing these points to score full marks.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd. (1897))
cases.text: The House of Lords held that an incorporated company is a **separate legal person** completely distinct from its shareholders. Even if one person holds nearly all shares, the company's **debts and liabilities** belong to the company itself, not the owner.

cases.name: State Trading Corporation of India v. CTO (1963))
cases.text: The Supreme Court of India held that a registered company is an **artificial legal person**, not a **citizen** under the Constitution of India. Therefore, a corporation cannot claim fundamental rights guaranteed exclusively to citizens under **Article 19**.

cases.name: SGPC v. Som Nath Dass (2000))
cases.text: The Supreme Court ruled that **Guru Granth Sahib** is a **juristic person** capable of holding property. The Court clarified that legal personality is a flexible concept developed by law to protect social, public, and **religious interests**.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paras: To conclude, **legal personality** is a vital tool of modern jurisprudence that extends legal recognition beyond human beings. While **natural persons** derive personality from birth, **artificial persons** receive it from law to facilitate commerce, charity, and governance. Understanding this distinction helps clarify how corporations, deities, and institutions function independently in Indian courts.

myth.myth: Only living human beings can own property or file a lawsuit in an Indian court.
myth.law: Law grants **legal personality** to entities like companies and idols, allowing them to **hold property** and **sue** in their own name.
myth.source_say: Under Section 9 of the Companies Act, 2013, an incorporated company becomes a separate legal person with power to hold property and sue.
myth.thumb: Can Non-Humans Own Property in India?

quiz.question: Which landmark case established the principle of separate corporate legal personality?
options: Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.
quiz.explain: **Salomon v. Salomon (1897)** held that an incorporated company is a **distinct legal person** separate from its shareholders and directors.

case.name: SGPC v. Som Nath Dass (2000))
case.facts: Revenue records mutated land in favour of Guru Granth Sahib. Respondents argued only living persons or deities, not a holy book, can hold property.
case.issue: Whether Guru Granth Sahib qualifies as a juristic person capable of holding property under Indian law.
case.held: The Supreme Court held that **Guru Granth Sahib** is a **juristic person** capable of holding property and protecting its rights through **granthis**.
case.principle: **Legal personality** is a creation of law granted to **non-human entities** to serve social and religious purposes effectively.
case.thumb: Can a Holy Book Own Land?

rows.label: Origin
rows.say: A natural person is born through nature, whereas an artificial person is created by law.

rows.label: Existence
rows.say: Natural persons have a physical body and mind, while artificial persons exist only in law.

rows.label: Lifespan
rows.say: A natural person dies physically, but an artificial person enjoys perpetual succession until dissolved.

rows.label: Fundamental Rights
rows.say: Natural persons can be citizens with full fundamental rights, unlike artificial persons.

compare.title: Natural vs Artificial Persons
